Fr. 14 καὶ παλτὰ κἀγκυλητὰ καὶ χλῆδον βαλών [and having thrown javelins and thonged spears and rubbish]. It is not clear what Aeschylus meant by χλῆδον [rubbish], whose words seem to Welcker in his book on the trilogies of Aeschylus p. 377 to be taken from a description of a battle. Demosthenes p. 1278 and 1279 said χλῆδον ἐμβάλλειν εἰς τὴν ὁδὸν [to throw rubbish into the road] of earth dug up and heaped on a road. The grammarians cited in Thes. vol. 8 p. 1526 noted that it is said of sweepings or shavings. Thus Harpocration, χλῆδος: πᾶν πλῆθος χλῆδος λέγεται, καὶ ἐστὶν οἷον σωρός τις, μάλιστα δὲ τὸ τῶν ἀποκαθαρμάτων τε καὶ ἀποψημάτων, καὶ ἡ τῶν ποταμῶν πρόσχωσις, καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον τῶν χειμάρρων, δ καὶ χέραδος καλεῖται [rubbish: every mass is called rubbish, and it is like a heap, especially of sweepings and scrapings, and the alluvial deposit of rivers, and much more of torrents, which is also called gravel]. Few examples of this word survive today, which Harpocration says many used.
